doc.title: Ted Piltzecker interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 10, 2019

title: Playing the Shearing sound: unison block-chord playing and its origin
summary: The front line played in unison with Shearing's locked hands; he says the vibes-guitar sound began as an octave error, and notes Shearing was criticized as polite.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: [percussive scats], as you know the way he would play is [percussive scats], but this was continuing, right, and the whole front line had to do that together. So George would be playing this lock hand position and the vibraphone and guitar had to play absolute unison with that, in that kind of — and there’s no way, it’s impossible. So you learn to listen in a really intense way. And after one or two times, and you didn’t rehearse. It was like the first, I’m doing this, there’s an audience and we’re trying to like negotiate — it’s terrifying. I saw one guitar player come onto the band, he turned white. I could see his face was white. I had been in the band for a year and he was doing the same thing. I had known the book by that point. So and then you get it. And then after a while you get it. So it’s a kind of, that nuanced application of time, the process of learning it was really hard, you have to listen so intensely. It’s like a tango people, not a tango show but a real tango dancer — I mean they are so tuned into each other and to the music. It’s just incredible.
Well that Shearing sound you know, that famous — was the vibe, were the vibes and the guitar usually playing the same octave or were you guys in octaves and is that what partly made that sound?
I think this was an error because as you know the guitar transposes an octave up. You write it an octave up.

So I think the guitar player played, when he wrote the music it came down. And I was playing with the piano and the guitar player, I believe that was an error in the beginning that became a sound and he milked it for a zillion years and it was a very cool thing. And he’s just a — I mean people call it “polite jazz.” During the height of his career he was criticized for being polite. It was too packaged. It was so, almost sweet. But this guy, I could tell you in simple terms, this guy could really play, and had an intellect that was incredible. And the story, sometimes I tell the story, he was playing with Andy Simpkins at a place called the Matador and he was using the quintet. It was Rusty Jones, Andy Simpkins, Billy Rodgers the guitar player from Omaha, myself and George. So he and Andy, George and Andy were playing at the Matador in San Francisco, and the next day the quintet was going on a tour, we were all getting on the bus and going to Seattle or something. So I walk into the club in San Francisco, and the manager goes over to George’s ear and says, “It’s a little tense here.” So he says to the audience, live, he says “Well our vibraphonist is here, we’re going to start our tour tomorrow with the quintet, and in Ted’s honor we’re going to play an arrangement that he did for the quintet.” I said great.
